name: Daria Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary factory shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead six people on the night bread line. I check dough moisture, the divider, the proving cabinet, the tunnel oven and the bagger before a batch leaves. I have a two-year technical diploma and can hear when the divider is chewing dough, but that skill has not brought a big wage here. I like the crew; the nights are hard on my sleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home alongside that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Sami drives a delivery van and takes our two children to school while I sleep. We have a mortgage, less than a month of expenses saved and almost no similar factory work nearby. Last year our mortgage payment rose, so even a normal month takes care. I use AI now and then to explain an unfamiliar fault code, but I make the safety call myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the bread crew that a few office shortcuts do not bake a batch or fix a wet dough mix. I would still ask why the plant spent on scheduling software before night-shift pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The line should stay, but our mortgage is already tight on my lower-than-average operator wage. We have less than one month saved and the next car repair could send us to credit. A quiet AI future would not cure that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading nights and ask our union steward to bring the shift-pay figures to the next plant meeting. I would apply for the posted day-lead vacancy only if it opens with a wage that covers our mortgage and the hours let me collect the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills even when the machines do little differently. I would still be glad to work a familiar line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changed in the mortgage payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fixed rate ended and the payment rose enough to wipe out what we used to save. I now keep the car repair money in mind whenever the children need new shoes. That is ordinary life before any robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you want the day-lead post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would see our children before dinner and sleep at night. The current lead has talked about leaving, but I need an actual posting and the wage before I make plans. A day shift with lower pay could hurt us more than nights.

say: I would **tell** the crew software does not replace the hands that bake and check bread.
I would **ask** why night-shift pay trails the cost of the new scheduler.
think: My **team-lead** skill keeps the line moving, but the mortgage already takes nearly all pay.
**Less** than one month saved makes even a small car bill serious.
do: **Keep** leading the night bread line and checking dough and oven temperatures.
**Ask** the union steward to raise night-shift pay figures.
**Apply** for posted day-lead work only if pay covers mortgage and hours fit childcare.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline household bills despite steady bakery work.
S0.quote: I would still ask why the plant spent on scheduling software before night-shift pay.
fieldNote: **Daria** is a skilled lead with a technical diploma but lower wages and a very thin cash reserve.
She **seeks** a day shift for family time only if a real vacancy and mortgage-covering pay exist.
Her **union** ask responds to present night-shift pay, not a speculative machine replacement.

steps.text: Keep leading the night bread line and checking each batch
Ask union steward to raise night-shift pay figures at plant meeting
Apply for posted day-lead work only if wages cover mortgage and hours fit childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management and the union to separate office scheduling changes from any later robot work on the bread line. Workers should get paid training before staffing is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could plan flour orders and shifts early while my crew still handles dough and jams. If the plant later uses robots to stack and clear more of the line, six people may become three. I could be kept as lead, but I cannot pay the mortgage on that guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a new AI production-scheduling tool on old shift data with the planner if the plant gives paid time and no live safety decision is delegated to it. I would ask for paid supervised line-maintenance training and enroll if offered with current wages and a posted lead-maintenance opening. I would attend the union staffing meeting while keeping my normal nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about being one of the three whose hours vanish. My line-lead experience gives me a chance, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust the planning tool after the old scheduler went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after it handles a full night roster without putting somebody on an impossible shift. The old system forgot that rest time is a human need. I would check every proposed roster before it reached the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid maintenance place is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the bakery wage while searching posted operator jobs within a workable journey. I would apply only if the pay covers the mortgage and the shift fits Sami’s school run. I would not spend our last savings on an unfunded course.

say: I would **ask** for paid training before any reduction in bread-line staffing.
**Office** scheduling software should be tested separately from later robot changes.
think: My **lead** experience helps, but a smaller crew could cut my own hours.
A **mortgage** with under one month saved cannot rest on being chosen for one remaining post.
do: **Practise** a new AI scheduler on old data only with paid time and human roster checks.
**Enroll** in paid supervised maintenance training only if offered with current wage and posted role.
**Attend** the union staffing meeting while keeping bakery shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about possible loss of hours despite strong line skills.
S1.quote: My line-lead experience gives me a chance, not a guarantee.
fieldNote: **Daria** treats her seniority as helpful but not enough to erase real staffing risk.
**New** AI scheduling practice is limited to old data, paid time and checked rosters after an earlier bad deployment.
A **paid** maintenance place requires supervision, current wages and a posted role; an unfunded fallback search has separate terms.

steps.text: Practise new AI scheduler on old data only with paid time and human checks
Enroll in paid supervised maintenance course only if offered with current pay and posted opening
Attend union meeting about bread-line staffing and paid training
Check posted operator jobs if no course and pay and school-run shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AGI in 2028 may take the planning desk before a capable robot can clear a bread jam. Robots that can handle the line arrive around 2031 in this picture, and we should ask for notice now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose most of my night-line hours around 2031 when robots can run the divider and bagger. Sami’s van route could also change when capable robots and automated delivery spread. With less than one month saved, two lost wages would leave the mortgage hanging, and I would lie awake at three checking the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Sami and I would list the mortgage, food and van costs, stop takeaways, and ask the lender about hardship terms before missing a payment. I would ask the union for written notice and redeployment terms. If a nearby hospital posts a paid kitchen-machine role after my line hours fall, I would apply only if the wage and shift cover our bills and school pickup; I would not count any support until eligibility is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about both wages. I can make calls and lists, but I would still be awake after a night shift doing the same sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at a hospital kitchen if robots arrive too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would only be a bridge while physical service still needs staff. I would not leave a bakery wage for a job title without a posting and a bill-covering offer. The kitchen machines may change later too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say we are cutting extras because work might change, not because they have done anything wrong. I would keep school meals before a holiday. Sami and I would decide together what else we can cover.

say: I would **ask** the plant for notice before capable line robots arrive around 2031.
The 2028 **thinking** AGI date may change bakery planning before physical production.
think: I **expect** major night-line wage loss around 2031.
**Sami’s** delivery earnings could weaken too, leaving our mortgage exposed with almost no reserve.
do: **Stop** takeaways and list mortgage, food and van costs with Sami.
**Ask** lender about hardship terms and union about written redeployment.
**Apply** for posted hospital kitchen-machine work only if pay and shift cover bills and pickup.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected two-income risk, awake checking the bank after shifts.
S2.quote: I would lie awake at three checking the account.
fieldNote: **Daria** expects the physical bread-line threat around 2031, after 2028 software changes to planning.
She does **not** presume public support or a hospital job, and requires a posted opening with adequate wages and school-compatible hours.
The **thin** reserve and possible two-income loss support alarm despite an orderly list of calls.

steps.text: Stop household takeaways and list mortgage food and van bills this week
Ask mortgage lender about hardship terms before a missed payment
Ask union for written notice and redeployment terms
Apply for posted hospital kitchen work only if pay and shift cover bills and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the bakery that five years allows a real training rota if it starts before the robot line is bought. AGI may plan orders by 2031, while robots that handle bread and cleaning follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 51 by the hands-on robot date, and the lead role may still shrink. I know the line better than most, but my lower wage leaves little room to buy a new trade. A paid course needs to fit the school run and my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply for the posted day-lead opening if it appears at mortgage-covering pay, then enroll in the college industrial-maintenance course only if the plant or union funds tuition, the new shift leaves evenings free and Sami can cover pickup. I would transfer a fixed amount from each actually paid overtime shift into savings while ordinary bills are covered. After training I would apply for a posted bakery-maintenance role only if its wage and shift cover the mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the future hours, but five years lets me check each condition before spending money. The plan works only if the day shift and funded course are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the day-lead post never opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would ask the college for a funded daytime option that fits my night rota; I would enroll only if an actual place and tuition funding are offered. If there is no workable course, I would search posted machine jobs on their own pay and school-hour terms. I cannot attend evenings after working through the night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much overtime would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with part of one extra shift each month when the mortgage and food are paid. There might be no extra shift in a quiet month, so the transfer would be zero then. I will not borrow money to say I am saving.

say: I would **ask** for a paid training rota before new robot equipment arrives.
The **day-lead** vacancy and funded course both need actual terms, not promises.
think: At 51 in 2034 my **lead** bread-line work might shrink.
My **lower** pay and thin reserve make unpaid study too risky.
do: Enrol in **funded maintenance training** with an offered place: evenings after a day-lead move and pickup cover, otherwise daytime fitting night shifts.
**Save** from newly paid overtime only after mortgage and food are covered.
Apply for **posted day-lead work**, qualified maintenance, or operator fallback, checking sufficient wages and school hours.
feel: **Anxious** about later hours, with time to verify a funded path.
S3.quote: I cannot attend evenings after working through the night.
fieldNote: **Daria’s** route depends on a posted day-lead job before an evening course can fit.
She **offers** a separate funded daytime course fallback if the day job fails, and a job search if no course works.
**New** saving comes from actual overtime shifts, with zero transfer in a quiet month.

steps.text: Apply for posted day-lead work only if wage covers mortgage
Take funded maintenance training: evenings after day-lead move and pickup cover, or daytime fitting night shifts
Save from paid overtime shifts only after mortgage and food are covered
Apply for posted bill-covering school-compatible maintenance after training or operator work if training fails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years is enough time for the plant to negotiate paid training and a fair shift plan, if it chooses to. I would raise that at the union meeting instead of hoping a poster fixes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 at the 2036 thinking-AI date and 56 when capable robots reach the bread line around 2039. The children will be older, but our mortgage may still need two wages. I would rather reach that date with a real maintenance wage than with a course badge and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a funded industrial-maintenance course with paid release time and supervised machine practice, then enroll if a place is offered and Sami can cover pickup. After qualifying I would apply for a posted local maintenance role only if its pay and shift cover the mortgage. Each month with paid overtime I would put a new amount toward the credit-card balance, while attending union meetings on future staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the long-run household wages, even with ten years. More time helps, but a thin reserve still makes every missed shift matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the bakery for another factory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a written offer that covers the mortgage and lets us manage the children’s evenings. There are not many similar jobs near us. I would not give up a steady night wage for a course the other plant may not recognise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to win first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid release for training, then a vacancy list with wages on it. I would ask about my crew as well as my own place. A six-person team cannot all become one maintenance operator.

say: I would **ask** for paid release and real maintenance vacancies through the union.
A **decade** should let the plant publish a fair staffing plan before capable robots arrive.
think: At 53 in 2036 I **may** still lead the bread line while planning software changes.
At 56 **near** 2039, I need a paid maintenance role if robots cut operator shifts.
do: **Enroll** in funded supervised maintenance training only if paid release and pickup are offered.
**Apply** after qualification only for posted local maintenance work with bill-covering pay and shifts.
**Pay** extra on the credit card from newly earned overtime.
feel: **Anxious** about household wages despite a longer warning and stronger plan.
S4.quote: A six-person team cannot all become one maintenance operator.
fieldNote: **Daria** uses a ten-year horizon to demand funded release time and a posted vacancy list, not a guaranteed transition.
Her **lower** wage and thin savings still make a missed paid shift serious.
**Extra** debt payment is conditional on new overtime earnings, while training also needs supervision and school pickup.

steps.text: Enroll in funded supervised maintenance course only with paid release and covered pickup
Apply for posted local maintenance work after qualification only if pay and shift cover mortgage
Pay extra credit-card principal only from newly paid overtime
Attend union meetings seeking paid release and a real vacancy list

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most because capable robots could cut my bread-line hours around 2031 while Sami’s delivery wage is also exposed. Immediate mortgage help if we qualify, paid shift-compatible training and written notice would help our family plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the children home when parents are sent to training. A nine-to-five course cannot serve a night crew whose day is for sleep.

headlineQuote: A nine-to-five course cannot serve a night crew whose day is for sleep.
portrait: **Daria** Petrov, 43, is a skilled night-shift lead at an industrial bakery with a two-year technical diploma.
She and **delivery-driver** partner Sami have two school-age children, a mortgage, lower operator pay and less than a month saved.
She **uses** AI occasionally, favours union action and checks whether paid training can fit night work and school pickup.
**Even** a plateau leaves her anxious about bills; later robot cuts threaten her six-person crew and two household wages.
She will **train** only with funding and workable shifts, and apply for real posted jobs with mortgage-covering pay.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI could cut her bread-line hours around 2031 while Sami’s delivery wage also weakens.
whatWouldHelp: **Mortgage** help if eligible, funded shift-compatible training and written notice of job changes would help.
